title: HeyGen API: Pricing, Features and How to Use It (2026)
summary: HeyGen API requires a key and involves tiered pricing and rate limits.
body_markdown:
## Call the HeyGen API without code in Activepieces


You don't need a developer to create videos and check their status in Activepieces, which has a HeyGen integration and a free plan with unlimited flows and 1,000 credits a month.


It's an automation tool where you chain steps together on a canvas instead of writing code, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has.


Polling is just one of those steps, which means the backup you keep is something you drag into place rather than program.


### Connect with your key


You paste the same HeyGen API key you would use in code into a new HeyGen connection in Activepieces, and that's the whole setup. Trying it costs nothing, since the free plan is $0 and needs no card.


Because it's the same key, nothing about your account changes. Every video the workflow creates draws from the same credit balance, and every call counts against the same concurrency limit.


When a no-code workflow fires on every form submission, it can burn through credits faster than a developer would, since nobody is watching the meter while it runs.


Set a cap on how often the trigger can fire before you switch it on, and check the current limits and credit costs on HeyGen's own pricing and API pages.


Expect gaps: **roughly 60% of Activepieces integrations are community-contributed** , so coverage follows what people have built, and the HeyGen integration won't cover every endpoint HeyGen offers.


When one is missing, Activepieces has a generic HTTP step that sends a request to any address you give it, using your key in the header.


That's your way around the gap, and it works the same as calling the API directly.


### Example: form submission to finished video


A form submission starts the workflow. A HeyGen step creates the video, a loop checks status until the render finishes, an HTTP step handles anything the integration lacks, and a Slack message posts the finished link.


That placement matters because rendering is asynchronous: the create step returns right away with an ID, not a finished file. Skip the loop and Slack gets a link to nothing.


Add a pause between checks and a limit on how many times the loop may run, so a stuck render ends in an error message instead of an endless loop.


From here, the remaining work is testing with a single submission and watching what it costs.
